Foreword

In Kenya, like in many developing countries, malnutrition continues to contribute to morbidity and
mortality concerns. More than half of the morbidity and mortality cases in children are attributable

the Government of Kenya, through the then Ministry of Public Health and Sanitation (currently Ministry
of Health), to institute the Kenya National Micronutrient Survey (KNMS) in 2011 to generate data on
factors.
from the Ministry of Health, Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) and Kenya National Bureau
Micronutrient Initiative, Global Alliance For Improved Nutrition, World Food Programme, Centre for
Disease Control and World Health Organization. Due to the nature of KNMS, covering both medical
and socio-demographic/economic investigations, KEMRI and KNBS as the government lead institutions
of the two types of surveys spearheaded its implementation.
establishing the prevalence of micronutrient malnutrition and selected infectious diseases related to
micronutrient interventions.

Dr. Yeri Kombe,
Principal Investigator,
KEMRI

                                                                        The Kenya National Micronutrient Survey 2011

Preface

surveys are necessary to understand the changes in the nutrition situation and accommodate new
information on dietary intake and micronutrients status of the population. Ideally, it is supposed to be

result of the interventions which have been put in place by the Ministry of Health and other supporting

A steering committee led by MoH Nutrition Unit and comprising of KEMRI, KNBS and key development
and implementing partners as lead members was constituted to plan for a national micronutrient survey
and ensure that it was properly implemented. In addition, the steering committee was charged with
fundraising for the survey. Alongside this committee, a technical committee led by KEMRI was established
which comprised of the technical personnel from MoH, KEMRI and KNBS, in collaboration with
UNICEF, MI, CDC, GAIN, WFP and WHO to design and implement the Kenya National Micronutrient
Survey.

collection, laboratory analysis and quality control and data analysis. Chapter three is on response rates

anaemia and associated factors. Vitamin A status is presented in chapter six while Iodine status and zinc
status results are presented in chapter seven and eight respectively. Chapter 9 discusses results on folate
and vitamin B12
recommendations for the report are presented in Chapter 11.

Dr. Jackson Kioko,                  Dr. Gerald Mkoji,

Dietary and Nutrient Intake                                  Conclusions and
                                                             Recommendations
The mean DDS in children was below the
recommended cut-off for minimum dietary                      Compared to the previous national micronutrient
diversity of at least 4 of the 7 food groups which           survey results, there is a considerable improvement
is associated with better quality for both breastfed         in the micronutrient status in Kenyan population
and non-breastfed children. Meat based-meals                 except for zinc deficiency whose prevalence
are least consumed by the households in the                  was higher. This may be attributed to the
poorest socio-economic index but the limited                 combined impact of the programs implemented
protein source appears to be compensated by                  by the Ministry of Health and partners. What
consumption of more beans and nuts among the                 requires to be done now is the scaling up of
poor. Grains were, in fact, important sources of             the implementation of high impact nutrition
all the micronutrients studied except for vitamin            interventions so that further gains can be realized.
A. Grains are the leading source of iron and zinc,
milk and dairy is the leading source of calcium,
and vegetables are the leading source of vitamin
A.

Notably, high salt consumption was noted by
about 90 percent of adults, and two-thirds of
children and the amounts were greater in adults
than children. Salt consumption appears similar
between urban and rural areas compared to sugar
where urban individuals consumed more sugar
than rural.

4.1. Overview                                            Weight-for-age is a composite index of height-for-
                                                         age and weight-for-height. It takes into account
The nutritional status of children has been              both chronic and acute malnutrition. Children
described using three indices namely, height             whose weight-for-age is below minus two standard
for age, weight for age and weight for height.           deviations (-2 SD) are classified as underweight.
Height-for-age index provides an indicator of            Children whose weight-for-age is below minus
linear growth retardation and cumulative growth          three standard deviations (-3 SD) are considered
deficits. Children whose height-for-age Z-score is       severely underweight (WHO, 2007).
below minus two standard deviations (-2 SD) from
the median of the WHO reference population are           4.2. Nutritional Status of
considered short for their age (stunted). Children               Children aged 6-59 months
who are below minus three standard deviations
(-3 SD) are considered severely stunted. Stunting        Nationally, the prevalence of stunting,
reflects failure to receive adequate nutrition           underweight and wasting in children aged 6-59
over a long period and is affected by recurrent          months was 26.3 percent, 12.7 percent and 6.3
and chronic illness. Height-for-age, therefore,          percent. Table 4-1 indicates the nutrition status of
represents the long-term effects of malnutrition in      children 6-59 months of age using height for age,
a population and is not sensitive to recent, short-      weight for age and weight for height.
term changes in dietary intake.

The weight-for-height index measures body                national levels of stunting reported in this survey
mass in relation to body height or length and            are classified as medium; so is the prevalence
describes current nutritional status. Children           underweight and wasting. A reduction in the
with Z-scores below minus two standard                   point prevalence was observed when these results

        anaemia                                            Hereditary blood disorders, also known as
                                                           heamoglobinopathies, constitute an important

and blood disorders are known to contribute to the         Sickle cell (SS) and thalassaemias are the two

blood loss and poor absorption of micronutrients.          in the beta globin gene located on chromosome

in the region. Other important tapeworms                   population with sickle cell disease is in Africa.
